title: Number of Connected Components
description: Given an undirected graph with n nodes labeled from 0 to n - 1 and an array of edges where edges[i] = [ui, vi] represents a connection between nodes ui and vi, return the number of connected components in the graph.

starter_code.typescript:
function countComponents(n: number, edges: number[][]): number {

sample_test_cases.explanation: The graph contains two connected components: {0,1,2} and {3,4}.

hints: Build an adjacency list for the graph.
Keep track of which nodes have already been visited.
Every time you start a new DFS/BFS from an unvisited node, you have found a new component.
Count how many independent traversals are required to visit all nodes.
explanation: A connected component is a group of nodes where every node is reachable from every other node in the group. Build an adjacency list and maintain a visited array. Iterate through all nodes. Whenever an unvisited node is encountered, perform a DFS or BFS to visit its entire component and increment the component count. After all nodes have been processed, the count represents the total number of connected components. The algorithm runs in O(V + E) time, where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges.

title: Number of Islands
description: Given an m x n 2D binary grid grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (water), return the number of islands. An island is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.

sample_test_cases.explanation: All land cells are connected, forming a single island.

hints: Treat each land cell as a graph node.
Two land cells are connected if they are adjacent horizontally or vertically.
When an unvisited land cell is found, explore its entire island.
Use DFS or BFS to mark all cells belonging to the same island.
explanation: Iterate through every cell in the grid. Whenever an unvisited land cell ('1') is encountered, increment the island count and perform a DFS or BFS to visit all connected land cells. Mark visited cells so they are not processed again. Each traversal completely explores one island. Since every cell is visited at most once, the algorithm runs in O(m × n) time with O(m × n) worst-case auxiliary space due to recursion stack or queue usage.

constraints: Node.val is unique for each node

sample_test_cases.explanation: The cloned graph has the same structure as the original graph but consists of entirely new nodes.

hints: You must create new nodes instead of reusing existing ones.
The graph may contain cycles.
Keep track of already cloned nodes.
A HashMap can map original nodes to their cloned counterparts.
explanation: Use DFS or BFS to traverse the graph. Maintain a HashMap where the key is an original node and the value is its cloned node. When visiting a node for the first time, create its clone and store it in the map. Then recursively or iteratively clone all of its neighbors and connect them to the cloned node. The HashMap prevents infinite loops caused by cycles and ensures each node is cloned exactly once. The algorithm runs in O(V + E) time, where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges.

You are given an array prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [a, b] indicates that you must take course b before course a. Return true if it is possible to finish all courses, otherwise return false.

hints: Think of courses as nodes in a directed graph.
A prerequisite relationship creates a directed edge.
Can all courses be completed if the graph contains a cycle?
Use DFS cycle detection or Topological Sorting.
explanation: Model the courses as a directed graph where an edge b → a means course b must be completed before course a. The problem reduces to determining whether the directed graph contains a cycle. If a cycle exists, the courses in that cycle depend on each other and cannot be completed. Use DFS with three states (unvisited, visiting, visited) to detect cycles, or perform Kahn's Topological Sort. If all courses can be processed without encountering a cycle, return true; otherwise return false. The algorithm runs in O(V + E) time.

title: Course Schedule II

You are given an array prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [a, b] indicates that you must take course b before course a. Return any valid ordering of courses that allows you to finish all courses. If it is impossible, return an empty array.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Course 0 must be completed before course 1.

hints: This is an ordering problem on a directed graph.
Nodes with no incoming edges can be taken immediately.
Track the indegree of every node.
Use Kahn's Algorithm (BFS Topological Sort).
explanation: Represent courses as nodes in a directed graph where an edge b → a indicates that course b must be completed before course a. Compute the indegree of every node and place all nodes with indegree 0 into a queue. Repeatedly remove a node from the queue, add it to the answer, and reduce the indegree of its neighbors. If a neighbor's indegree becomes 0, add it to the queue. If all courses are processed, the generated order is a valid topological ordering. If some nodes remain unprocessed, a cycle exists and no valid ordering is possible, so return an empty array. The algorithm runs in O(V + E) time.

title: Rotting Oranges
description: You are given an m x n grid where each cell can have one of three values: 0 representing an empty cell, 1 representing a fresh orange, and 2 representing a rotten orange. Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes required until no fresh orange remains. If this is impossible, return -1.

sample_test_cases.explanation: All fresh oranges become rotten after 4 minutes.

hints: All rotten oranges start spreading simultaneously.
Think of each rotten orange as a BFS starting point.
Place all initially rotten oranges into the queue before starting BFS.
Process the grid level by level, where each BFS level represents one minute.
explanation: This is a Multi-Source BFS problem. Instead of starting BFS from a single source, add all initially rotten oranges to the queue at the beginning. Count the number of fresh oranges. During each minute (BFS level), rotten oranges infect their adjacent fresh neighbors. Whenever a fresh orange becomes rotten, add it to the queue and decrease the fresh count. After BFS completes, if fresh oranges still remain, return -1 because some oranges are unreachable. Otherwise, return the number of minutes required. Each cell is processed at most once, giving O(m × n) time complexity.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect All Points
description: You are given an array points where points[i] = [xi, yi] represents a point on a 2D plane. The cost of connecting two points is the Manhattan distance between them: |xi - xj| + |yi - yj|. Return the minimum cost required to connect all points such that there is exactly one simple path between any two points.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The minimum spanning tree connects all points with a total cost of 20.

hints: Treat every point as a graph node.
The cost between two points is their Manhattan distance.
You need to connect all nodes with minimum total cost and no cycles.
This is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) problem. Prim's Algorithm is a good choice.
explanation: The problem asks for the minimum total cost required to connect all points while ensuring every point remains reachable. This is exactly the definition of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST). Using Prim's Algorithm, start from any point and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects a new point to the growing MST. Maintain the minimum connection cost for every unvisited point and always select the point with the smallest available cost. Once all points are included, the accumulated cost is the answer. The algorithm constructs an MST and guarantees the minimum possible total connection cost.
